title: Lina and the Lost Map
markdown:
The Northwind Heights always held a quiet magic, especially when the moon painted the snowy peaks with gentle silver. The air itself seemed to hum with a soft wonder. Frost sparkled on the evergreen branches like fallen stars, and the snow crunched underfoot with a happy sound. Lina, a young elf with eyes like dewdrops and hair the colour of pale moonlight, felt a familiar quiet flutter in her heart. It was a feeling that often visited her when the moon was high and bright. Tonight it felt especially strong. It was time, she decided, to ask the Old Pine Tree a question. A very important question that had been tickling her thoughts like a gentle breeze.

“Corvus,” she whispered, her voice as soft as the sigh of the wind. Corvus, her glossy black crow, her loyal friend, was perched on her shoulder. His feathers shimmered in the moonlight, looking as if he were wearing a tiny fancy suit. “It’s time. The Old Pine Tree is waiting.”

Corvus ruffled his feathers, a sound like dry leaves rustling. “A question. A grand question, indeed,” he squawked, his head bobbing. “What is it, Lina? Is it about the juiciest berries? Or perhaps why the moon smiles so much at us little creatures?” His voice was a cheerful jumble of squawks, like a happy music box.

Lina giggled, a sound like tiny silver bells dancing. “It’s a bit more important than berries, Corvus. And the moon’s smile is a lovely thought, but you’ll see when we get there.” She gave his glossy head a gentle pat.

And so they set off into the tinkling pine woods. Every step crunched softly on the needles. The air smelled wonderfully of sweet pine and crisp winter, a scent that made your lungs feel clean and happy. Little lights from the forest folk’s homes twinkled like fallen stars through the trees, casting soft welcoming pools of light. But Lina and Corvus were on a special journey, guided by the moon. The pine trees, tall and wise, seemed to hum a soft tune as they passed.

As they rounded a bend where the moonlight fell in patches, like a lace doily on the forest floor, they heard a lot of rustling and a soft muffled “Oh, dearie me.”

Sitting on a mossy log, looking very confused, was a small goblin. He was no bigger than Lina’s boot, and he wore a flour-dusted apron. His pointed ears were dusted with white, just like his nose, and he wriggled them. In his hands he held a very crumpled and confusing-looking map.

“Good evening,” called Lina, her voice as soft as a moth’s wing. She never wanted to startle anyone.

The goblin jumped, then blinked his wide kind eyes. They were the colour of warm honey. “Oh. Well, hello there, little elf. And you too, feathered friend,” he chirped, his voice squeaky like a new gate opening. “I’m Gnorman. Gnorman the Goblin Baker. And I seem to have gotten lost, even though I’m standing right here.” He patted the log he was sitting on.

Corvus hopped to a low branch, tilting his head as if considering a hard puzzle. “Gotten lost? Are you sure you’re not just very, very still, Gnorman? Perhaps you’ve turned into a statue.”

Gnorman wrung his floury hands, which made little puffs of white dust dance in the moonlight. “That’s just it. This map,” he unfolded it with a sigh that sounded like a gentle gust of wind. It showed a drawing of squiggles and dots that looked more like a sneeze on paper than a path. “It’s for the bestest mountain lantern. My Auntie Hildegard says it’s the most important lantern for finding the juiciest dewberries to make her special moonbeam tarts. But it says ‘turn left at the sleepy squirrel’ and all the squirrels are awake and nibbling nuts, and then ‘follow the wobbly star’ and all the stars are quite straight and proper.”

Lina peered at the map, her brow furrowed in gentle thought. Corvus fluttered closer, his sharp eyes picking out details. He even pecked gently at a particularly wiggly line.

“This isn’t a path to follow, Gnorman,” Lina said kindly, pointing a small finger at the map. “Look, these are drawings of the things for the lantern. See? This big squiggle here… that’s the moonpetal that glows with a soft light, like the one we saw earlier. And this little dot is a sleepy firefly for its light, so it twinkles just right. And this wiggly line… it’s not a path. It looks like a stream, doesn’t it?”

Gnorman’s eyes widened, and he leaned closer, his flour-dusted ears twitching. “A stream. Of course. My stream. The Willow Creek. It does get a bit wobbly near the bend by the old oak tree.” He looked at the map with new understanding, his confusion melting away like butter on a warm scone. “So I don’t follow it… I just need to find the stream itself, where it wiggles, to make the lantern’s glow?”

“Exactly,” Lina beamed, her face lighting up like a tiny sun. “And you’ll find the dewberries, the ones that taste like sweet starlight, near where the stream sparkles brightest, especially when the moon is out.”

Gnorman clapped his hands together, a sound like two small dough balls meeting. He did it again, sending another puff of flour into the air, making him look even more like a happy snowy owl. “Oh, thank you, Lina. And thank you, wise Corvus. You’ve untangled my muddled thoughts. It’s like you’ve smoothed out all the tangles in my brain.” He carefully folded the map, and now it seemed much clearer, like a perfectly written recipe. “Now I must be off to collect the moonpetal from the meadow by the creek. And perhaps I can bake you both a little something as a thank you? A tiny star cookie, maybe?”

Lina smiled, a warm sweet smile that could melt any winter frost. “That’s very kind, Gnorman. But our question is almost answered, and home will be so cosy with Mama’s warm cocoa waiting for us.” She knew her mother would be happy to see her back, safe and sound.

Gnorman nodded, gathered his supplies — a little wicker basket and a small wooden spoon — and with a happy “Happy baking” from Corvus, he scurried off into the trees, his little lantern-making journey now clear and bright.

Lina and Corvus continued their walk, the air filled with the gentle jingling of unseen pine cones nudged by the breeze and the soft silvery glow of the moon. They soon reached the Old Pine Tree. It was magnificent, its ancient branches reaching like welcoming arms towards the sky, its bark rough and wise. It stood like a watcher over the forest.

Lina stood at its trunk, her heart feeling light and full. She did not need to speak the question aloud. The crumpled map had already used it up, in the kindest way. The quiet flutter in her heart settled into a gentle happy hum.

Corvus landed on her head, his familiar weight a comforting presence, like a warm cap. “Home, Lina? The bestest place of all? Where the fire is always crackling and the stories are always warm?”

Lina nodded, a soft smile reaching her eyes. “Yes, Corvus. Home.”

As they turned back towards the warm glow of their own little home, nestled safely in the heart of the Northwind Heights, the forest seemed to sigh. The moonlight was a soft comforting blanket, and the path back was familiar and safe. Mama’s cocoa would still be waiting. Gnorman’s stream would still wobble by the oak. The Old Pine did not need to be asked twice, which was how you knew a sneeze of a map could still point to tarts.
characters: Lina (young elf of the Northwind Heights), Corvus (a glossy black crow)
